2. Read the following passage carefully and answer the question that follows.
In every field of life—be it sports, academics, music, or business—the discussion of talent
versus hard work often arises. Some people believe that natural talent is the primary reason for
success, while others argue that hard work plays a far more significant role. Talent refers to the
natural ability that one is born with. For example, a person may have a natural talent for singing or
mathematics. Such individuals often learn things faster and perform better at an early stage.
However, relying solely on talent without consistent effort can be a mistake. History is full of
examples where talented individuals did not achieve great heights because they lacked dedication
and discipline. On the contrary, many people with average ability have excelled through determination,
constant practice, and hard work. One such example is Thomas Alva Edison, who had limited formal
education but became one of the greatest inventors due to his perseverance.
Hard work not only improves skills but also builds character. It teaches discipline, time
management, and patience. While talent can give an initial advantage, it is hard work that sustains
long-term success. Moreover, hard-working individuals tend to be more adaptable and better prepared
to face challenges, making them valuable assets in both personal and professional life.
Employers and organizations increasingly value employees who show commitment, persistence,
and a willingness to learn. In today’s competitive world, talent alone is no longer enough. The
combination of effort, attitude, and continuous learning often outweighs pure natural ability. In
conclusion, while talent may open doors, it is hard work that keeps them open.

3. Read the following passage carefully and write a precis in about one third of its length. Suggest a
suitable title.
(10)
In our modern society, academic degrees are often seen as the primary measure of a person’s
intelligence and capability. From an early age, students are encouraged to pursue higher education,
with the promise that a degree will ensure a successful and prosperous future. Employers frequently
prioritize candidates with formal qualifications, and society places high esteem on those who have
studied at reputed institutions. However, this growing dependence on degrees has led to the
undervaluation of something equally, if not more, important—common sense.
Common sense refers to the ability to make sound judgments based on practical knowledge
and everyday experiences. It is not something that can be taught in textbooks or classrooms. While
education equips individuals with theoretical knowledge, it does not always prepare them for real-life
challenges. Many highly educated people struggle when faced with everyday problems that require
practical thinking, while others with little formal education navigate these situations with ease. For
instance, a person might hold an advanced degree in business management but still lack the basic
understanding of dealing with people or handling unforeseen circumstances.
Moreover, common sense often leads to innovation and creativity. Some of the most successful
entrepreneurs and leaders in history did not possess extensive formal education but excelled because
of their sharp instincts, decision-making ability, and practical wisdom. This is not to undermine the
value of education—it is undoubtedly important—but it should be complemented by real-world
understanding.
In conclusion, while a degree might open doors, common sense is what helps individuals make
the most of those opportunities. Success in life is not solely determined by academic achievements,
but also by one’s ability to think clearly, make wise choices, and respond effectively to challenges.
Both education and common sense are valuable, but relying solely on degrees can be misleading.
